James Talarico and the Art of the Walk-Back
 
Plus, the U.S. pulls its B-1 bombers from U.K. air base, and there is plenty of friction as the Supreme Court begins a new term
 
 
BRANDON BELL/GETTY IMAGES
 

Good morning. Republican Ken Paxton had one thing going for him early on in his Senate race against Democrat James Talarico: Talarico’s own words.

 

So why is Talarico still ahead in many Texas polls?

 

The 37-year-old Democrat has said plenty of controversial things, and in a way, he is sort of owning them. He has acknowledged that some of his past comments are “cringey” and is essentially asking for Texans’ understanding.

 

This is an approach that Vice President JD Vance used quite effectively during the 2024 campaign. Vance was hit hard for some of the things he had said in the past on television or podcasts, including the “childless cat ladies” quip. 

 

During the vice presidential debate, Vance and Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz (the Democratic candidate) both owned having said things in the past they’d rather have back (whether it worked for Walz or not is unclear).

 

One of Talarico’s biggest eyebrow-raisers occurred in 2021, when he said “God is both masculine and feminine and everything in between. God is nonbinary.”

 

Earlier this year, Talarico told CBS he was being “intentionally provocative with that statement.”

 

“There are some statements that I made that I certainly regret,” he said. “Statements that I’ve made where I’ve missed the mark.”

 

Owning it. That doesn’t always happen in politics.

 

Still, this can be tricky stuff. Republicans really hammered John Kerry in 2004 for his “flip flops.” 

 

Politicians are notorious for opportunistically changing their views on things (the current data center freakout is a great example of this).

 

Sometimes it works (politically). Sometimes it doesn’t.

 

This is an edition of the Politics newsletter, bringing you an expert guide to what’s driving D.C. every day. If you’re not subscribed, sign up here.

 
 
 

People and Policies I’m Watching

 

Supreme Court: The high court begins its new term on Monday.

 

Trump’s Monday: President Trump is scheduled to hold several policy meetings at the White House. Later, he will travel to Grand Island, Neb., to take part in a midterm rally.

What I’m Following

 
 
DAVID BOWN/GETTY IMAGES
 

U.S. removes its bombers from British base. The U.S. removed all its B-1 bombers from the U.K.’s RAF Fairford air base, due to security concerns over suspected plots to attack the facility. The U.S. has used the military base as a hub for launching bomber strikes in Iran. Until their recent departure, a dozen B-1s had been stationed at the base.

 

The Supreme Court returns for a new term. As the Supreme Court begins its new term, Trump has renewed his periodic attacks on the justices’ integrity. Leading Democrats, eyeing the 2028 election, are embracing proposals to blunt the court’s conservative bent by adding more members. Among the public, the court’s approval rating is underwater. And there are signs of friction between the high court and the lower courts it supervises.

 

Democrats work to fend off challenges in blue states. Senate seats in states that Trump won comfortably are now seen as tossups, and House seats that he carried by double digits are in danger of flipping. At the same time, Democrats are struggling to coalesce around an ideological platform and face a steep financial disadvantage to Republicans. In some blue-leaning states, Senate GOP candidates are staging strong challenges.

 
 
 

What Else Is Happening

 

• Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Josh Hawley are opening a probe into how leading home and auto insurers process claims.

 

• Flávio Bolsonaro dealt Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva a bruising first-round defeat, leaving the incumbent with an uphill fight ahead of an Oct. 25 runoff.

 

• Many voters say energy prices are on their minds as they head to the ballot box in November for the midterms.

 

• Americans are spending more on food, travel, couches, and most anything else they want or need—pushing through inflation and their own feelings about the economy.
